narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Binary Search, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 50, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.

narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Binary Search, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 16 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 31, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(log n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Arrays, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 97, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Arrays, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 2, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: A single linear scan keeps a running best value; it costs n-1 comparisons and no extra space. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 10 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 13, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Arrays, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 0, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Arrays, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 0, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Sorting, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 7 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n^2) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

The run is bounded by O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n^2) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Sorting, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 5 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n^2) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Sorting, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 5 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n^2) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Scan the unsorted suffix for the minimum, then swap it into place; exactly n-1 swaps regardless of input. The run is bounded by O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

actionMeaning.selectObject: take a lantern in hand — the read operation. Mechanically: Click/tap a single object to read it, pick it as the current item, or make it the mid/target.
actionMeaning.comparePair: inspect two lanterns against each other — the compare operation. Mechanically: Select two objects and declare lt / eq / gt between their values.
actionMeaning.swapPair: trade places between two lanterns — the swap operation. Mechanically: Exchange the positions of two objects.
actionMeaning.submitAnswer: commit the obsidian vault — the terminate operation. Mechanically: Commit the final answer: declare the result index, value, or outcome.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Sorting, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 7 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n^2) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Sorting, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n^2) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.

Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.

Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 10 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Add to the top, never into the middle. A stack has no middle to add to.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Pushing every opener and popping on each closer makes mismatches obvious at the top of the stack. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Stack, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 7 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Add to the top, never into the middle. A stack has no middle to add to.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.

narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Stack, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Add to the top, never into the middle. A stack has no middle to add to.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Queue, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 7 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Add to the top, never into the middle. A stack has no middle to add to.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(1) per op in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: A queue is FIFO: enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front, and front/rear wrap around in a circular buffer. The run is bounded by O(1) per op time and O(n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.

Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Arrays, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 12 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n log n) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Binary Search, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 7 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 70, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(log n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Binary Search, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 9 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 97, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(log n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Linked List, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: There is no counting along a chain of links — you can only follow one. Each step forward is exactly one link followed.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Move one link at a time. You cannot skip ahead and you cannot look back without starting over.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.

narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: A fast pointer gains one node per round on a slow pointer, so on a cycle they must eventually meet; on a plain list the fast pointer runs off the end. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Trees, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 5 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Add to the top, never into the middle. A stack has no middle to add to.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(w) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Trees, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 9 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Add to the top, never into the middle. A stack has no middle to add to.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(w) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Trees, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 5 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 88, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.

narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Heap, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 9 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n log k) in the worst case, O(k) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.

hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.

The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: The ways to reach step i reuse smaller answers: step 1 or 2 at a time means ways[i] is the sum of the two previous counts. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 5 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 7 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.

Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Backtracking, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 4 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n × 2^n) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Backtracking, and it has to be done by the book. hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.

narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Greedy, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 5 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.

Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 9 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(amount × coins) in the worst case, O(amount) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 11 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(amount × coins) in the worst case, O(amount) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 5 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(E log E) in the worst case, O(V) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Graphs, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(E log E) in the worst case, O(V) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 16 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(rows × cols) in the worst case, O(rows × cols) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 25 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(rows × cols) in the worst case, O(rows × cols) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: The ways to reach a cell reuse smaller answers: add the ways from above and from the left — a blocked cell contributes zero. The run is bounded by O(rows × cols) time and O(rows × cols) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 25 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(rows × cols) in the worst case, O(rows × cols) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: The ways to reach a cell reuse smaller answers: add the ways from above and from the left — a blocked cell contributes zero. The run is bounded by O(rows × cols) time and O(rows × cols) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

actionMeaning.selectObject: take a lantern in hand — the read operation. Mechanically: Click/tap a single object to read it, pick it as the current item, or make it the mid/target.
actionMeaning.assignValue: write a value into the obsidian vault slot — the assign operation. Mechanically: Set a value into a slot, container or variable (e.g. running max, complement, sum).
actionMeaning.submitAnswer: commit the obsidian vault — the terminate operation. Mechanically: Commit the final answer: declare the result index, value, or outcome.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 30 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(rows × cols) in the worst case, O(rows × cols) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 16 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(m × n) in the worst case, O(m × n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 20 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(m × n) in the worst case, O(m × n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 25 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(m × n) in the worst case, O(m × n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 16 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(m × n) in the worst case, O(m × n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 20 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(m × n) in the worst case, O(m × n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Turning one string into the other reuses smaller answers: a match copies the diagonal for free, otherwise pay one plus the cheapest of deleting, inserting, or substituting. The run is bounded by O(m × n) time and O(m × n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 25 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(m × n) in the worst case, O(m × n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.
